Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims

Reuters

17 October, 2026 05:30 am IST

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Steve Holland and Kanishka Singh DALTON, Georgia, Oct 16 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran’s presidency during a campaign speech on Friday.

“You know, if you’re in doubt about somebody’s name from the Middle East, just say ‘Mohammad,'” Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. “You have about a 65% chance. ‘Hello, Mohammad.’ I’ve done it for years now. I’ve never been wrong.”

Mohammad is one of the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Show Full Article

Trump made the comment as he was discussing Iran during a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

“Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president,” Trump said, then pretended to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian has been president of Iran since 2024.

The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response.

Rights advocates and Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.

He has escalated such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee.

Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program.

An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year attributed rising Islamophobia in the US in part to Trump’s crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.

(Reporting by Steve Holland in Dalton, Georgia, and Kanishka Singh and Jarrett Renshaw in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman)

Russian attacks kill eight in Ukraine, cut power to over a million

Reuters

17 October, 2026 04:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

KYIV, Oct 16 (Reuters) – Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 across Ukraine on Friday, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than 1 million people after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.

A 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man died and 12 more people were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.

Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine people, officials said.

Show Full Article

Attacks in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in Donetsk Region killed two people and two more were killed in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk Region.

Ukraine’s energy ministry said its repair crews had returned power to over 1 million people who had lost it as a result of Russian attacks on Friday. It was not clear how many were still without power.

In the northwestern region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk. He said 370,000 people were temporarily without power in the morning, although 100,000 of them got supply back later on.

The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn’s regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.

Romaniuk said that drone attacks continued throughout the day, striking a customs terminal and torching about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, which sits on a major trunk road from Kyiv to Poland.

Other attacks hit at least two shopping centres — one in the northern city of Sumy, which lies close to the front line, and one in the neighbouring region of Rivne, officials said — the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.

Pictures from emergency services in Sumy showed blood spattered across the floor and shots of the centre’s damaged entrance.

One person was killed and seven wounded by drones that hit a major shopping centre and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.

Ukraine’s energy ministry said large parts of the city of Rivne and the surrounding area were without power after attacks on energy infrastructure there.

(Reporting by Max Hunder, Lina Golovnya and Yuliia Dysa; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Ron Popeski and Sanjeev Miglani)

Teacher tackled and fought Oregon school shooter

Reuters

17 October, 2026 04:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) – A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said on Friday.

A day into their investigation of the latest U.S. school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.

Show Full Article

“She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Krantz said.

As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.

Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school, upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter was dead, police said.

In the meantime the 16-year-old assailant, who had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.

Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, “I don’t think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that.”

He said that the bystander’s actions “undoubtedly saved people,” and “the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that’s true heroism.”

Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him.

The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother told the New York Times. She identified him as the father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said. “Kaylub’s family, including his two daughters who attend the school, respectfully asks for privacy during this difficult time, and will not be participating in interviews at this time.”

Residents of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles just outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.

“Thank God for that father. He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today. We wish him well, and thank God for him,” Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears.

Brooke Olsen, the mother of a kindergartener who was safely reunited with her family after the shooting, also expressed gratitude for the man who stopped the shooter.

“This is an extremely painful day of grief for everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families, and we have to think about what’s next for safety measures.”

Such school shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debates over gun laws in a country where a right to “keep and bear Arms” is protected under the Constitution’s Second Amendment.

Some of the deadliest school attacks in the US include those at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018 and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.

(Reporting by Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom in Bend; Additional reproting by Jonathan Allen in New York and Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Paul Thomasch and Jonathan Spicer)

Missiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu

Reuters

17 October, 2026 03:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Oct 16 (Reuters) – Missiles struck Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.

The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.

In Aden, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-aligned Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility.

Show Full Article

No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.

Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.

Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.

Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.

Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country’s humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.

The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen’s war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.

The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.

A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as “Saudi aggression” since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

(Reporting by Enas Alashray, Mohammed Ghobari, Ahmed Tolba and Yasmine Ghania; Writing by Enas Alashray; Editing by Alison Williams and Cynthia Osterman)
